Boltz-Flow: Generating High-Quality Robot Action from Boltzmann Machine

Hengzhi Jiang, Haixu Liu, Jindou Jia, Tinglan Wang, Shaobo Chen, Yiren Zhao, Ziyang Rao, Laiyuan Cui, Jiaxin Dong, Yin Ma, Hai Wei, Jiaqi Bai, Tuo An, Xinyu Zhou, Hao Ban, Hongdong Zhu, Yanqi Wang, Jiaqi Dou, Nuo Qian, Qi Liu, Bin Jin, Chang Wu, Qingfeng Li, Hui Yang, Weiyu Guo, Dicong Qiu, Qi Gao, Jianwei Niu, Kai Wen, Jianfei Yang
Beijing QBoson Quantum Technology Co., Ltd.   Beihang University   Nanyang Technological University   The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)   Quantsparkle.ai   The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Abstract

Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves π0.5\pi_{0.5} across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.

1 Introduction

The long-term goal of robot learning is to enable robots to acquire and execute general-purpose physical skills in open-world environments. With large-scale robot datasets and vision-language pretraining, vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a key paradigm connecting scene perception, language understanding, and robot control [27]. VLAs, such as RT-2 [60] and OpenVLA [27], discretize continuous actions into tokens and generate them autoregressively [34]. For continuous action generation [24], diffusion policy [10] casts action synthesis as iterative denoising. Flow matching [32] instead learns a conditional velocity field that transports a Gaussian source distribution to the action distribution. VLAs such as π0\pi_{0} [5] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [4] combine such a flow-matching action expert with a pretrained vision-language backbone and generate generalizable actions.

However, the Gaussian source is specified by design rather than learned from data, although it fully determines where flow integration starts [32]. This limits flow policies in two ways. The first is capacity. An isotropic Gaussian is unimodal and identical for every task, scene, and instruction, so its probability mass cannot shift toward the actions that a particular observation calls for. As datasets broaden and horizons lengthen, the expressiveness of the starting point, rather than the capacity of the velocity field, likely becomes the limiting factor. The second is coupling. The source is sampled independently across time steps and control dimensions, whereas position, orientation, and gripper motion must stay coordinated across an entire action chunk. Condition-to-action [55] and action-to-action [23] sources each relax one limits. However, both narrow the source around a single predicted start and thus trade representational capacity for conditioning [22]. A better source should therefore be conditioned on the observation, coupled across variables, and still expressive enough to hold several action modes.

To this end, we turn to the Boltzmann distribution. A Boltzmann machine (BM) naturally supports multimodal distributions and captures richer dependencies than a standard Gaussian [16, 42]. Moreover, recent quantum computing devices, such as the coherent Ising machine (CIM) [51], have renewed interest in applying Boltzmann models to deep learning [6, 48]. This raises a fundamental question for robot learning. Can robot actions be generated from a Boltzmann distribution instead of simple Gaussian noise to achieve stronger manipulation performance? This work answers it in the affirmative. We propose Boltz-Flow, a Boltzmann-based robot Flow policy that generates high-quality actions from a learnable, observation-conditioned, and variable-coupled source distribution (Fig. 1). To exploit the action dependencies in demonstrations, Boltz-Flow follows the maximum-entropy principle and builds an instance-specific Gibbs–Boltzmann energy landscape for each observation. This landscape assigns higher probability to low-energy structured sources and makes no unsupported assumptions about the geometry of the remaining action modes.

Concretely, Boltz-Flow instantiates this source with a conditional BM. A multimodal encoder maps the image, instruction, and robot state to a representation that parameterizes a dense quadratic energy over a binary encoding of the initial source. For a fixed observation, this energy is an Ising instance. The CIM searches its low-energy configurations, and its programmable all-to-all connectivity matches the couplings across time steps and action dimensions. We use the CIM for this search during training, and simulated annealing (SA) can replace it at inference to reduce latency. The returned state is decoded into continuous noise, from which the frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} runs its original ten-step integration. The action is thus still produced entirely by the pretrained velocity field. Training uses offline demonstrations alone. We rank candidate sources by how far the resulting frozen-policy actions deviate from the expert action, and a listwise objective aligns the energy landscape with this ranking. At test time, low energy alone identifies a high-quality source.

We evaluate Boltz-Flow on LIBERO [33], LIBERO-Plus [14], and RoboTwin 2.0. Across the 40 LIBERO tasks, CIM-trained Boltz-Flow raises the average success rate of π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 94.65% to 98.55%, and subsequent noise-adapted fine-tuning raises it to 99.05%. On LIBERO-Plus, it improves the seven-category average from 82.3% to 85.9%, an absolute gain of 3.6 percentage points (pp), with improvements in all 7 categories. On RoboTwin 2.0, it increases success rates from 78.68% to 80.82% under clean conditions and from 54.54% to 56.92% under randomized conditions. CIM-based training also converges in fewer iterations than SA-based training on LIBERO. Moreover, the gains stack with action-to-action initialization [23] and transfer to the SmolVLA backbone [41].

2 Related Work

Source Initialization for Flow Policies.

Flow-matching VLAs generate actions by transporting a source distribution to the action distribution, and the initial noise sets the boundary condition of this finite-step integration [32]. In general generative modeling, prior work improves the starting point by learning noise transformations, searching or selecting initial noise, and predicting context-dependent Gaussian priors [37]. In robot action generation, existing initialization strategies fall into four categories. Unconditional initialization samples from an observation-independent standard Gaussian and remains the default in π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [5, 4]. Learning-based structured initialization builds a starting point with richer action structure from the task context [55, 13]. History-based initialization exploits temporal continuity and builds the next starting point from previous actions [23, 22]. Noise-space selection and adaptation search, filter, invert, or learn the starting point in the input space of a frozen policy [47]. Unlike these strategies, Boltz-Flow learns a source that is conditioned on the observation, coupled across time steps and action dimensions, and able to hold several low-energy modes at once.

Quantum Computing for Energy-Based Models.

Quantum annealers have been used to estimate the negative-phase statistics of BMs and to train hardware-embedded probabilistic graphical models [2]. CIMs encode spins with optical parametric oscillators and realize densely connected Ising optimization through time multiplexing and measurement-feedback coupling [21]. Noise-injected optoelectronic Ising machines further support approximate Boltzmann sampling and restricted BM training [6]. Quantum BMs define energy models through quantum Gibbs states [1]. Boltzmann priors for the latent variables of variational autoencoders (VAEs) have been implemented with quantum Monte Carlo, D-Wave annealers, and CIMs [25, 46, 48]. D-Wave-sampled Boltzmann priors have also replaced random latent variables in generative adversarial networks (GANs) [52]. These works target generic generative models and their training. In contrast, Boltz-Flow uses a CIM to search the source of a robot policy, which is, to our knowledge, the first use of a quantum computer for continuous robot action generation.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

Flow matching [32] is a representative generative paradigm for continuous-control VLAs [4, 5]. Given the robot observation ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O} and language instruction l∈ℒl\in\mathcal{L}, where 𝒪\mathcal{O} and ℒ\mathcal{L} denote the observation and instruction spaces, it integrates a conditional velocity field over flow time τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]. The integration transports a source sample at τ=0\tau=0 into an action chunk of H∈ℕH\in\mathbb{N} steps and da∈ℕd_{a}\in\mathbb{N} action dimensions at τ=1\tau=1. Let 𝓖θ\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{\theta} denote the complete KK-step numerical integration (K∈ℕK\in\mathbb{N}) of the learned velocity field with parameters θ\theta. Standard generation is written as

𝐚^=𝓖θ​(ot,l,ϵ),ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈),\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{\theta}(o_{t},l;\boldsymbol{\epsilon}),\qquad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), (1)

where the initial noise ϵ∈ℝH×da\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}} follows the Gaussian distribution and 𝐚^∈ℝH×da\hat{\mathbf{a}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}} is the predicted action chunk.

This noise is independent of the observation and instruction, and independent across time steps and control dimensions. However, for a fixed observation and a frozen policy, different noise samples produce action chunks whose errors with respect to the demonstration vary substantially. We therefore replace the fixed Gaussian prior with a condition-dependent noise sampler 𝓢ψ\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}_{\psi},

ϵ~=𝓢ψ​(ot,l,𝝃),\tilde{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}_{\psi}(o_{t},l;\boldsymbol{\xi}), (2)

where ψ\psi denotes the sampler parameters, 𝝃∈Ξ\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\Xi represents its internal randomness with sample space Ξ\Xi, and ϵ~∈ℝH×da\tilde{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}} is the generated noise. This noise replaces ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon} in 𝓖θ\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{\theta}, and the policy stays frozen. This formulation covers learned latent-noise policies, deterministic initializers, and energy-based samplers. Our goal is a sampler that assigns higher probability to noise that produces lower-error actions.

Boltz-Flow instantiates 𝓢ψ\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}_{\psi} with a conditional BM, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The observation and instruction define an energy over binary states, and Ising search returns low-energy states. A midpoint-Gaussian-quantile mapping turns the selected state into continuous noise, from which the frozen policy generates the action chunk without any change to its velocity field. Sec. 3.2 details this source, and Sec. 3.3 describes how it is trained.

3.2 Boltzmann Flow-Matching Policy

Conditional Boltzmann Machine.

Rather than regressing continuous noise directly, the BM models a distribution over binary states through its energy landscape. A multimodal Transformer encodes the observation and instruction into a fixed-length representation 𝐳=𝐟ϕ​(ot,l)∈ℝV\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{f}_{\phi}(o_{t},l)\in\mathbb{R}^{V}, where ϕ\phi denotes the encoder parameters and V∈ℕV\in\mathbb{N}. We treat 𝐳\mathbf{z} as the visible condition nodes of the BM and let 𝐡∈{0,1}Nh\mathbf{h}\in\{0,1\}^{N_{h}} denote its Nh∈ℕN_{h}\in\mathbb{N} binary hidden nodes. With the complete state 𝐱=[𝐳;𝐡]∈ℝV+Nh\mathbf{x}=[\mathbf{z};\mathbf{h}]\in\mathbb{R}^{V+N_{h}}, the conditional energy is

Eψ​(𝐳,𝐡)=−𝐱𝖳​𝐛−𝐱𝖳​𝐐𝐱,E_{\psi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{h})=-\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}, (3)

where 𝐐∈ℝ(V+Nh)×(V+Nh)\mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{(V+N_{h})\times(V+N_{h})} is the quadratic coupling matrix and 𝐛∈ℝV+Nh\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{V+N_{h}} is the linear bias. We write ψ={ϕ,𝐐,𝐛}\psi=\{\phi,\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{b}\} for all learnable parameters. With the visible nodes clamped to 𝐳\mathbf{z}, the energy induces the conditional Boltzmann distribution

𝐡^∼pψ​(𝐡∣𝐳)=exp⁡[−Eψ​(𝐳,𝐡)]Zψ​(𝐳),\hat{\mathbf{h}}\sim p_{\psi}(\mathbf{h}\mid\mathbf{z})=\frac{\exp[-E_{\psi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{h})]}{Z_{\psi}(\mathbf{z})}, (4)

where 𝐡^∈{0,1}Nh\hat{\mathbf{h}}\in\{0,1\}^{N_{h}} is a sampled hidden state and the partition function Zψ​(𝐳)>0Z_{\psi}(\mathbf{z})>0 normalizes over all binary states. Lower-energy states thus receive exponentially higher probability. Because the landscape can hold several separated low-energy basins, sampling can return states from distinct modes. The source therefore stays diverse while adapting to the current observation and instruction.

Ising-Based Sampling.

For a fixed 𝐳\mathbf{z}, collecting all terms that depend on 𝐡\mathbf{h} gives the binary quadratic energy

E𝐳​(𝐡)=C⁡(𝐳)+∑a=1Nhαa​(𝐳)​ha+∑1≤a<a′≤Nhβa,a′​ha​ha′,E_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{h})=C(\mathbf{z})+\sum_{a=1}^{N_{h}}\alpha_{a}(\mathbf{z})\,h_{a}+\sum_{1\leq a<a^{\prime}\leq N_{h}}\beta_{a,a^{\prime}}h_{a}h_{a^{\prime}}, (5)

where C⁡(𝐳)∈ℝC(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R} does not depend on 𝐡\mathbf{h}, αa​(𝐳)∈ℝ\alpha_{a}(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R} is the condition-dependent linear coefficient of hidden node aa, and βa,a′∈ℝ\beta_{a,a^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R} is the coupling between hidden nodes a,a′∈{1,…,Nh}a,a^{\prime}\in\{1,\ldots,N_{h}\}. The standard affine bit-to-spin map sa=2​ha−1∈{−1,+1}s_{a}=2h_{a}-1\in\{-1,+1\} turns Eq. (5) into an equivalent Ising problem with local fields and pairwise spin couplings. This conversion preserves the ordering of hidden states up to an additive constant and any positive rescaling that the hardware requires. Finding the lowest-energy state is NP-hard. We therefore use the CIM [51], a quantum-optical computer for Ising optimization. It carries computation on coherent photonic states and efficiently explores low-energy configurations of large Ising systems. The CIM returns one or more low-energy spin configurations, which are mapped back to binary states 𝐡^\hat{\mathbf{h}}. The full coefficient transformation and the augmented-matrix construction are given in the supplementary material.

From Binary States to Noise.

The BM uses

Nh=H​de​BqN_{h}=Hd_{e}B_{q} (6)

binary variables, where de∈ℕd_{e}\in\mathbb{N}, de≤dad_{e}\leq d_{a}, is the number of action dimensions modeled by the BM, and Bq∈ℕB_{q}\in\mathbb{N} is the number of Gray-code bits per noise coordinate. Each group of BqB_{q} bits is decoded into an integer κ∈{0,…,2Bq−1}\kappa\in\{0,\ldots,2^{B_{q}}-1\} and mapped to the midpoint Gaussian quantile Φ−1​((κ+1/2)/2Bq)\Phi^{-1}((\kappa+1/2)/2^{B_{q}}), where Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is the inverse cumulative distribution function of the standard Gaussian. The remaining da−ded_{a}-d_{e} dimensions keep independent standard Gaussian values. The resulting noise ϵ⁡(𝐡^)∈ℝH×da\boldsymbol{\epsilon}(\hat{\mathbf{h}})\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}} is injected once as the initial state of 𝓖θ\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{\theta}. Neither the input of the velocity field nor the integration procedure changes.

CPU–GPU–CIM Execution.

The pipeline splits the work across three processors. The GPU runs the Transformer that produces 𝐳\mathbf{z}, evaluates the differentiable BM energies during training, and generates the actions. The CPU runs the policy loop, exchanges sensor and action data with the environment, builds the Ising instance ℐ\mathcal{I} from 𝐳\mathbf{z}, calls the solver, and decodes the returned set of spin configurations 𝒴⊆{−1,+1}Nh\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^{N_{h}}. The CIM receives only the Ising coefficients and never processes raw images, language instructions, or gradients. The resulting data flow is

ot\displaystyle o_{t} →GPU𝐳→CPUℐ→CIM𝒴,\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\mathrm{GPU}}\mathbf{z}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CPU}}\mathcal{I}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CIM}}\mathcal{Y}, (7)
𝒴\displaystyle\mathcal{Y} →CPU𝐡^→GPU𝐚^→CPU/GPUenvironment.\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CPU}}\hat{\mathbf{h}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{GPU}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CPU/GPU}}\mathrm{environment}.

Only the combinatorial search thus runs on the CIM, while perception, learning, action generation, and environment interaction stay on the classical CPU–GPU system.

3.3 Training Objective

We train the BM with supervision from the frozen policy. For each tuple (ot,l,𝐚⋆)(o_{t},l,\mathbf{a}^{\star}) drawn from the demonstration dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, where 𝐚⋆∈ℝH×da\mathbf{a}^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}} is the expert action chunk, we build a candidate set {𝐡k}k=1M⊂{0,1}Nh\{\mathbf{h}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{M}\subset\{0,1\}^{N_{h}} of M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N} states. It mixes low-energy states proposed by the BM with random states. Each state is mapped to noise for the frozen generator, 𝐚^k=𝓖θ​(ot,l,ϵ⁡(𝐡k))∈ℝH×da\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{\theta}(o_{t},l;\boldsymbol{\epsilon}(\mathbf{h}_{k}))\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}, with θ\theta fixed.

We score each candidate by its error on the ded_{e} action dimensions modeled by the BM, ek=(H​de)−1​‖𝐚^k,e−𝐚e⋆‖F2∈ℝ≥0e_{k}=(Hd_{e})^{-1}\|\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k,e}-\mathbf{a}^{\star}_{e}\|_{F}^{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, where the subscript ee selects these dimensions so that 𝐚^k,e,𝐚e⋆∈ℝH×de\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k,e},\mathbf{a}^{\star}_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{e}}. The error is a stop-gradient signal and does not backpropagate through 𝓖θ\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{\theta}. To remove scale differences across examples, we standardize the errors within each candidate set as e~k=(ek−μe)/(σe+ν)\tilde{e}_{k}=(e_{k}-\mu_{e})/(\sigma_{e}+\nu), where μe∈ℝ\mu_{e}\in\mathbb{R} and σe∈ℝ≥0\sigma_{e}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} are their mean and standard deviation and ν>0\nu>0 ensures numerical stability. The standardized errors define target weights, and the energies define model probabilities over the same set,

wk\displaystyle w_{k} =exp(−e~k/Te)∑j=1Mexp(−e~j/Te),\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(-\tilde{e}_{k}/T_{e})}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}\exp(-\tilde{e}_{j}/T_{e})}, (8)
pψ,k\displaystyle p_{\psi,k} =exp⁡[−Eψ​(𝐳,𝐡k)]∑j=1Mexp⁡[−Eψ​(𝐳,𝐡j)],\displaystyle=\frac{\exp[-E_{\psi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{h}_{k})]}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}\exp[-E_{\psi}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{h}_{j})]},

where wk,pψ,k∈(0,1)w_{k},p_{\psi,k}\in(0,1) and the temperature Te>0T_{e}>0 controls how concentrated the target weights are. A listwise cross-entropy aligns the two distributions,

ℒnoise=𝔼[−∑k=1Mwklogpψ,k]+λℛ(ψ),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{noise}}=\mathbb{E}\left[-\sum_{k=1}^{M}w_{k}\log p_{\psi,k}\right]+\lambda\mathcal{R}(\psi), (9)

where the expectation runs over training examples and candidate sets, and ℛ⁡(ψ)∈ℝ≥0\mathcal{R}(\psi)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is a regularizer with coefficient λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. The BM thus learns to assign lower energy to states whose noise yields better actions after frozen integration, without updating the base policy.

4 Experiments

We evaluate Boltz-Flow on LIBERO [33], LIBERO-Plus [14], and RoboTwin 2.0, comparing it with strong imitation learning baselines and state-of-the-art source initialization methods. Controlled ablations examine the effects of the initial source distribution and full-parameter fine-tuning. We then compare task success rates across hardware solver backends used for training and inference, analyze training convergence efficiency, and study the impact of Gray-code precision. We further assess cross-backbone transfer to SmolVLA [41] and composability with Action-to-Action [23]. Finally, we conduct real-world robot experiments on five tasks adapted from RoboTwin 2.0 to compare the manipulation performance of Boltz-Flow and OpenPI.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and metrics.

We evaluate Boltz-Flow on standard LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0. LIBERO has 4 suites, Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long, with 10 tasks per suite. We follow the standard training protocol and conduct 50 evaluation rollouts per task, totaling 2,000 rollouts per method. LIBERO-Plus applies 7 controlled perturbations, Camera, Robot, Language, Light, Background, Noise, and Layout, to the same 40 tasks and contains 10,030 evaluation instances. LIBERO-Plus is used exclusively for testing. We report the success rate of each suite and their mean. RoboTwin 2.0 [9] contains 50 bimanual tasks. We conduct 100 rollouts per task in each of the Clean and Random settings and report the mean task success rate(SR).

Policy backbones and evaluation protocols.

Our primary backbone is the OpenPI implementation of the π0.5\pi_{0.5} flow-matching policy [4]. We distinguish two settings. Boltz-Flow trains the conditional energy-based noise module while keeping the policy frozen. Boltz-Flow + noise-adapted full fine-tuning subsequently updates all π0.5\pi_{0.5} parameters to adapt the velocity field to the learned source distribution. Controlled comparisons use the same action normalization and 10-step Euler integration budget. The execution horizon r∈{1,…,H}r\in\{1,\ldots,H\} denotes the number of predicted actions executed before the policy is queried again. We set both the prediction horizon HH and the execution horizon rr to 10 for the controlled comparisons below. To accommodate the CIM’s capacity of 1,000 spin variables, we encode each noise component using 7-bit Gray codes for bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (da=14d_{a}=14) and 14-bit Gray codes for single-arm LIBERO tasks (da=7d_{a}=7). Both settings use Nh=980N_{h}=980 binary variables. FT denotes subsequent noise-adapted full fine-tuning of the corresponding policy. Given limited access to CIM resources, we use the CIM as the training-time energy solver only on LIBERO. The resulting models are evaluated on LIBERO with both CIM and SA inference, and on LIBERO-Plus with SA inference. RoboTwin 2.0 experiments use SA for energy minimization during both training and inference. The supplementary material reports additional solver diagnostics. We reproduce LEAP, VITA, Fast-Flow, and A2A with the OpenPI π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone, training each method for 30,000 optimization steps with a global batch size of 32. LEAP updates the base policy, whereas VITA, Fast-Flow, and A2A keep it frozen.

4.2 Benchmark Results

LIBERO. Table 1 separates reported results from our OpenPI evaluations. Frozen Boltz-Flow achieves 98.6% average success, surpassing the strong baselines and prior state-of-the-art methods for source-distribution optimization, with a 1.3 percentage-point lead over A2A. It improves over OpenPI (94.7% average) on all four suites, with the largest gain on Long-Horizon (87.6% to 96.4%). Noise-adapted fine-tuning further raises average success to 99.1%.

LIBERO-Plus. Table 2 shows that frozen Boltz-Flow raises Overall success from 82.3% to 85.9%, improving all seven categories. The largest gains are in Light (+5.5) and Background (+5.3), followed by Language and Layout (+4.4 each). Noise-adapted fine-tuning reaches 87.3%, improving five categories over frozen Boltz-Flow, with the largest gain in Noise (+5.5). Light decreases from 97.4% to 97.2%, and Background from 97.9% to 97.1%. The selected self-evaluated baselines achieve 87.5% (LEAP), 86.1% (VITA), 85.8% (A2A), and 85.2% (Fast-Flow) Overall.

RoboTwin. RoboTwin 2.0 [9] is evaluated under Clean and Random settings. Clean uses the standard configuration. Random applies the full set of benchmark randomizations, including color changes, variations in natural-language instructions, and distractor objects. Table 3 separates reported results from our OpenPI evaluations. The reported baselines use 50 Clean demonstrations per task and are evaluated on 50 tasks with 100 trials per task in each setting [36, 40]. VITA freezes the base policy, whereas LEAP allows it to be updated. Boltz-Flow improves both settings over OpenPI. With noise-adapted fine-tuning, it reaches 81.28% and 57.56% on Clean and Random, respectively, the highest rates among the listed methods.

4.3 Ablation Studies

4.3.1 Initial Source Distribution

Table 4 isolates the effect of the initial source distribution under the same OpenPI backbone. A VAE source raises average success from 94.65% to 96.55%, showing that learning an observation-dependent initialization is already useful. Boltz-Flow reaches 98.10%, improving over standard Gaussian noise by 3.45 points and over VAE noise by 1.55 points. The difference is most pronounced on Long-Horizon: VAE noise reaches 92.8%, whereas Boltz-Flow reaches 96.2%, a further gain of 3.4 points.

This ablation locates the key benefit in the structure of the source rather than in learned noise alone. Under partial task constraints, the observation-conditioned Gibbs–Boltzmann distribution can reweight several low-energy initial configurations while its pairwise energy terms capture dependencies across time steps and control dimensions. The especially large Long-Horizon gain is consistent with this joint representation: multi-stage tasks place stronger demands on the coordination of position, orientation, and gripper control throughout an action block.

4.3.2 Training Strategy and Noise Adaptation

Table 5 compares Boltz-Flow with full-parameter fine-tuning. Frozen Boltz-Flow reaches 98.10%, outperforming the OpenPI baseline by 3.45 pp and full-parameter fine-tuning by 0.35 pp. A conditioned source thus improves access to control priors in the frozen VLA. Noise-adapted fine-tuning raises success from 98.10% to 98.70%. Object and Long-Horizon each gain 1.2 pp, reaching 99.8% and 97.4%. Boltz-Flow improves the initial source, and fine-tuning adapts the velocity field to it, making the stages complementary.

4.3.3 Training Solvers and Efficiency

Solver convergence.

Figure 3(a,b) compares the training convergence of CIM and SA on standard LIBERO. Panel (a) shows checkpoint success rates and their three-point moving averages, with peak success rates of 98.6% for CIM and 98.1% for SA. Panel (b) reports the best success rate attained up to each training iteration. CIM reaches the 97.0% and 98.0% success thresholds after 1,000 and 5,000 iterations, respectively, compared with 2,500 and 12,000 iterations for SA. These correspond to reductions of 60.0% and 58.3% in the number of training iterations required to reach the respective thresholds. The Train and Infer columns in Tables 6 and 7 specify the training and inference solvers, respectively; the main benchmark results use CIM for training and SA for inference on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and SA for both stages on RoboTwin 2.0. On LIBERO, replacing SA training with CIM training raises average success from 98.1% to 98.6% with the policy frozen, and from 98.7% to 99.1% after noise-adapted fine-tuning. Using CIM at inference further raises the frozen model’s success to 99.0%. On LIBERO-Plus, CIM training raises Overall success from 85.4% to 85.9% with the policy frozen, and from 86.8% to 87.3% after noise-adapted fine-tuning.

4.4 Parameter Studies

4.4.1 Gray-Code Precision

Figure 3(c) shows how success varies with the number of Gray-code bits per noise coordinate. Mean success remains close to the 14-bit reference down to 7 bits. Reducing the width from 14 to 7 bits halves the number of binary source variables in Eq. (6), from 980 to 490 at fixed H=10H=10 and de=7d_{e}=7. Mean success decreases from 98.10% to 97.85%, a drop of 0.25 percentage points. More aggressive precision reduction incurs larger losses, with the heatmap identifying Long-Horizon as the most sensitive suite. This suggests that moderate source compression preserves most of the policy’s success, while finer source resolution is more consequential for long-horizon tasks. The reduction applies to the binary source representation; the frozen velocity field is unchanged.

4.5 Composability and Transfer Test

4.5.1 Transfer to SmolVLA

Using the reproduced SmolVLA as the controlled baseline, Table 8 shows that Boltz-Flow raises success from 91.05% to 92.90%. The gains are positive on every suite: +2.6 on Spatial, +0.2 on Object, +2.8 on Goal, and +1.8 on Long-Horizon. This cross-backbone improvement shows that Boltz-Flow is not tied to the particular velocity-field implementation of OpenPI and can improve the source interface of another flow-matching VLA.

4.5.2 Compatibility with Action-to-Action

Table 9 tests whether Boltz-Flow can improve an existing action-level warm start. The combination improves the A2A average from 97.30% to 97.95% (+0.65), with Long-Horizon increasing by 1.6 points to 95.4% and positive increments on all four suites. Thus, Boltz-Flow can can be used alongside an action warm start and continues to improve the match between the initial distribution and the current task.

4.6 Real-World Robot Experiments

We compare the OpenPI implementation of π0.5\pi_{0.5} with Boltz-Flow on 5 real-world robot tasks: placing medicine into a tray using both arms, stacking three bowls, handing over a block between the two arms, placing a can next to a pot, and scanning a barcode. We collect 200 demonstration trajectories per task, totaling 1,000 demonstrations. Each model is evaluated over 10 trials per task, totaling 50 trials per model. Table 10 reports per-task and mean success rates, together with Boltz-Flow’s gains over OpenPI. Boltz-Flow increases the overall success rate from 46% to 62%, an absolute gain of 16 percentage points. It improves all 5 tasks. The largest gains occur in can placement (+30 pp). These improvements across multiple tasks support the practical benefit of learned source initialization for real-world manipulation.

5 Conclusion

Boltz-Flow learns an observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source for flow-matching policies. A listwise objective from offline demonstrations aligns source energy with action quality, enabling Ising optimization to select the initial state for a single flow integration. With π0.5\pi_{0.5} frozen, Boltz-Flow improves performance on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, with particularly strong gains on LIBERO-Long. Controlled ablations support the effectiveness of source learning and its complementarity with noise-adapted fine-tuning. These gains extend to SmolVLA, compose with action-to-action initialization, and persist across five real-world manipulation tasks. On LIBERO, the physical CIM benefits both training and inference: compared with GPU-based SA, CIM-assisted training achieves higher final policy success and reaches matched success thresholds with 58.3%–60.0% fewer training iterations, while CIM inference further improves task success. These results demonstrate that source-distribution learning improves pretrained policies while preserving their standard flow integration, and that CIM-based energy optimization further enhances training convergence and inference performance.
